context_after.text: The Fe $2 p _ { 3 / 2 }$ and the Mo 3d peaks were deconvoluted into a metallic and an oxidized part without subdividing the latter into different valence states. The average atomic fraction of the Fe, Cr and Mo cations in the film was calculated using the area sensitivity factors of Table 3. The results are summarized in Fig. 6. The cathodically polarized sample (CA) contains significantly more Fe than the anodically polarized samples (PL) and (PH). Similarly, more molybdenum is present on the cathodically polarized sample (CA) than on the passivated samples. The concentration of Fe, Cr and Mo in the metal layers just underneath the film was estimated for the two alloys,15, but because such data are subject to considerable uncertainty they will not be discussed here. Indeed, the absolute value of the calculated metal concentration underneath passive films depends heavily on the procedure used for peak deconvolution and background subtraction and on the precision of the values of the electron mean free path employed.

Figure 11 shows measured XPS spectra of (a) sulfur and (b) chloride, respectively. A well pronounced S 2p signal is apparent for the anodically polarized samples (PL) and (PH) but not for the cathodically polarized sample (CA). The energy of the peak corresponds to that of hexavalent sulfur. Similarly, a Cl 2p peak is observed for the samples (PL) and (PH) but not for the sample (CA). The peak energy is approximately 199 eV in reasonable agreement with published data¹ for chloride ion (198-199) eV. The measured intensity of the Cl 2p signal was too weak for quantitative analysis. The sulfur concentration in the film could be determined quantitatively. The apparent sulfur concentration in the passive films (PL) and (PH) on both alloys was found to be 3–5% for both potentials and electrolytes used. The data indicate that sulfate ions are incorporated in the passive film during its formation. The absence of a significant sulfur concentration on the (CA) samples is consistent with the fact that surface films in this case form mostly outside the electrolyte after completion of the polarization experiment.

context_after.text: profiles. Figure 12 shows AES profiles (corrected for escape depth) of the S LMM peak at 152 eV for the polarization conditions (CA) and (PH) in electrolyte B. The data confirm qualitatively the XPS results; the signal intensity for the samples (PH) is much higher than for the samples (CA). The sulfur profiles of the Fe-24Cr and the Fe-24Cr–11Mo alloys differ, sulfur being present in deeper layers of the passive film on Fe-24Cr. It may be recalled that the thickness of the oxide films under these conditions is approximately the same for the two alloys (Fig. 5).

A chloride AES profile could be measured on the Fe-24Cr alloy only because of interference of the Mo MVV peak at 186 eV with the Cl LMM peak at 181 eV. Figure 13 shows measured profiles corrected for escape depth for three polarization conditions in electrolyte B. On the sample (CA) a weak Cl signal is observed at the outer surface, probably resulting from a contamination or from incomplete removal of electrolyte during rinsing. The samples (PL) and (PH) contrary to (CA) exhibit a well pronounced maximum of the Cl signal at a distance of approximately 0.4 nm from the outer film surface. From this it may be concluded that the passive films formed by anodic polarization in electrolyte B contained chloride ions. The shape of the profiles indicates that they were located predominantly in the outer part of the film.

context_after.text: SIMS is not impeded by other species. Figure 15 shows negative SIMS profiles of chloride (mass/charge ratio 35) on (a) Fe-24Cr and (b) Fe-24Cr-11Mo, respectively. On the Fe-24Cr alloy polarized at (CA) Cl− is detected at the outer film surface only. The signal is attributed to adsorbed chloride in agreement with AES data. On the same alloy polarized at (PL) and (PH), respectively, the maximum signal intensity is located in the interior of the film, the effect being most pronounced for the condition (PH). On Fe–24Cr–11Mo (Fig. 15b) a similar behaviour is observed but the chloride maxima for (PL) and (PH) are closer to the outer film surface. Qualitatively, the SIMS profiles of Fig. 15(a) are in good agreement with the AES results of Fig. 13. This indicates that the shape of the SIMS profiles is not significantly disturbed by matrix effects and is indeed representative of the variation of concentration with depth.

The characterization of passive films by AES, XPS and SIMS is subject to the limitations inherent in all ex situ methods.¹ An important consideration, therefore, is to what extent results are affected by the rinsing and sample transfer procedures used and what reproducibility can be achieved. The former point has been discussed elsewhere.15,18 Suffice here to mention that SIMS experiments performed with the $^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { O }$ isotope indicate that at potentials (PH) the post-oxidation of passive films is negligible. For the potentials (PL) such experiments are not available but it may be reasonably supposed that the behavior is similar. The presented data for (PH) and (PL), therefore, are believed to be representative of the passive film. The (CA) data, on the other hand, represent the film formed in air during rinsing and transfer and their reproducibility is limited. It is clear from a comparison of the results that the chemical composition of the two types of films differs substantially.
